title: Human Sovereignty in the Agentic City: Enforcing Multi-Sector Capability Floors Against Automated Deprivation
content: Municipalities increasingly delegate healthcare, social assistance, utilities, transit, and identity verification to semi-autonomous systems. Real-world failures, including Australia's Robodebt scheme and the Dutch childcare benefits scandal, show that automated administration can strip life-sustaining services from large populations whose formal entitlements never changed. Existing governance responses remain fragmented across sectoral silos, with none enforcing a computationally verified constraint at the individual level across multiple domains concurrently. We present \HSC{}, a multi-agent framework that operationalizes essential human functioning as a non-compensatory constraint on automated municipal allocation. The architecture establishes a per-resident capability floor over ten normalized dimensions, identifying deprivation via an Alkire--Foster dual cutoff so that surplus in one domain cannot offset deficits in another. A Human Sovereignty Gate evaluates candidate allocations by measured worst-case capability impact and reversibility, recording commitments in an auditable ledger for which we prove that no admissible sequence of automated decisions can cross the floor. A Basic Needs Assurance Engine coordinates sector agents over a cyclic dependency graph to block cross-sector cascades, backed by an offline resilience reserve during platform outages. We derive a feasibility bound showing that individual risk tolerance cannot be legislated to zero, and specify an agent-based evaluation protocol for 250{,}000 synthetic residents across six disruption scenarios.
